title: Metabolic-inflammatory heterogeneity in PCOS assisted reproduction: a compartmental susceptibility model.
abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a heterogeneous endocrine-metabolic disorder rather than a uniform reproductive diagnosis. Women entering assisted reproductive technology (ART) differ in adiposity, insulin sensitivity, lipid metabolism, androgen excess, inflammatory activity, and oxidative stress, but these systemic traits do not map uniformly onto the follicular or endometrial compartments. We propose a testable compartmental susceptibility model in which systemic metabolic-inflammatory burden acts as a background exposure and clinically relevant effects emerge when stage-specific follicular-oocyte or endometrial-maternal vulnerability is also present. Evidence was interpreted with a pragmatic hierarchy that separates guideline/RCT evidence, registry and externally validated prognostic evidence, adjusted observational associations, mechanistic discovery studies, and protocol-only evidence. Current data support metabolic assessment, prevention of excessive ovarian response, and maternal risk surveillance, but they do not validate a metabolic-inflammatory subtype for selecting stimulation, trigger, frozen-embryo-transfer preparation, immune adjuncts, or other phenotype-specific treatment. Local immune, extracellular-vesicle, and multi-omics signals remain discovery tools rather than clinical tests. Precision ART in PCOS will require paired systemic-local phenotyping, external validation, and prospective phenotype-by-treatment interaction studies using cumulative live birth and maternal-neonatal safety as primary endpoints.

title: Paternally Inherited DIO3 Loss and Infantile-Onset Central Hypothyroidism: Human Evidence for a Novel Mechanism of Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Thyroid Axis Dysregulation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: DIO3 encodes type 3 iodothyronine deiodinase, the major thyroid hormone-inactivating enzyme, and is an imprinted gene with preferential paternal-allele expression demonstrated in human neonatal skin. Dio3-deficient mice develop neonatal thyrotoxicosis followed by central hypothyroidism, but human evidence has been lacking.
PATIENT FINDINGS: On newborn screening, thyrotropin (TSH) and free thyroxine (fT4) did not meet repeat-testing criteria, while T-cell lymphopenia was detected neonatally. From 5 months onward, fT4 progressively declined without compensatory TSH elevation. Chromosomal microarray identified a derivative chromosome 14 with a 14q32.31-q32.33 deletion encompassing DIO3 and TRAF3. The deletion originated from a paternal balanced 4p/14q translocation.
SUMMARY: In this patient, delayed-onset central hypothyroidism was most consistent with paternal DIO3 loss, whereas the accompanying T-cell lymphopenia was consistent with TRAF3 haploinsufficiency.
CONCLUSIONS: This case provides the first human evidence linking paternal DIO3 loss to delayed-onset central hypothyroidism, supporting a novel developmental mechanism that may alter hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis programming.

title: Technology use in youth with type 1 diabetes and language of care other than English.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Our primary aim was to describe continuous glucose monitor (CGM) and insulin pump use in youth with T1D with a preferred language of care other than English (LOE) and examine associations between diabetes technology use and hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) in this population.
METHODS: We assessed baseline technology use for youth with LOE and T1D seen in diabetes clinics at a single center between February 2022 and February 2023. A two-sample t-test was used to compare HbA1c values between groups. A linear regression model was used to examine differences in HbA1c between the 3-level technology groups with Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons.
RESULTS: Ninety-four youth with T1D and LOE with complete data on technology use were included in analysis. At baseline 66 % were using diabetes technology with 42 (45 %) using CGM only, 1 (1 %) using insulin pump only, 19 (20 %) using both insulin pump and CGM, and 32 (34 %) not using any technology. HbA1c was significantly lower in the technology use group (Mean=9.1 %, SD=2.4) compared to the non-technology use group (Mean=10.5 %, SD=2.2) (p=0.01).
CONCLUSIONS: Despite advances in technology for diabetes management, about one-third of youth with T1D and LOE were not using any diabetes technology. Diabetes technology use in this group was associated with lower HbA1c. Further work should be done to increase diabetes technology use in youth with T1D and LOE.

title: Case Report: Case series: growth hormone replacement for severe growth hormone deficiency during BRAF inhibitor therapy in pediatric low-grade glioma: long-term follow-up.
abstract: Pediatric low-grade gliomas (pLGGs) involving the hypothalamic-pituitary region frequently result in endocrine dysfunction, particularly growth hormone deficiency (GHD), due to tumor location and treatment-related effects. Growth hormone replacement therapy (GHRT) is generally considered after a period of disease stability, whereas its use during active oncologic therapy remains controversial, including during BRAF inhibitor (BRAFi) treatment. We describe two pediatric patients with severe GHD who received GHRT during ongoing vemurafenib, a BRAFi, for progressive chiasmatic-hypothalamic pLGG. The first patient, a girl diagnosed in infancy with desmoplastic infantile ganglioglioma, developed severe GHD after biopsy, chemotherapy, partial tumor debulking, and targeted therapy, together with multiple additional endocrine deficiencies. The second patient, a boy with pilocytic astrocytoma, was diagnosed with severe GHD after multimodal treatment, including partial and subtotal surgical resections, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted therapy. In both cases, low-dose GHRT was initiated after multidisciplinary assessment, documented radiological stability before GHRT initiation, and family counseling regarding the absence of direct safety data during active BRAFi therapy. Treatment was titrated over two months, with regular IGF-1 monitoring and close endocrine and oncologic surveillance. During approximately six years of concomitant GHRT and vemurafenib exposure, growth stabilized and lipid parameters improved, whereas catch-up growth remained limited and bone outcomes were complex, with increased bone mineral content but persistent or worsening lumbar DXA-derived impairment. No tumor progression or secondary malignancies were detected during the reported follow-up. These two cases add to the limited evidence on GHRT administration during BRAFi therapy by documenting prolonged concomitant GHRT and vemurafenib exposure in children with severe confirmed GHD and previously progressive chiasmatic-hypothalamic pLGG. However, the limited sample size and observational nature of this report preclude conclusions about safety or efficacy. Larger prospective studies are needed to define which patients may benefit and under which monitoring conditions GHRT could be considered during BRAFi therapy.

title: Maternal gestational weight gain and offspring vitamin D level: a multicentre retrospective cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study examined the association between maternal gestational weight gain (GWG) and offspring vitamin D levels.
METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, 0-5-year-old children attending routine health checks at 12 centres across 10 cities in Jiangsu Province (April 2014-March 2015) were enrolled via stratified random cluster sampling. Serum 25(OH)D was measured by ELISA.
RESULTS: Among 1,984 mother-offspring pairs, GWG ≤10 kg was associated with an increased risk of vitamin D deficiency (<50 nmol/L) in the unadjusted model (OR = 1.550, 95% CI: 1.196-2.008), and this association remained significant in Model 1 (OR = 1.820, 95% CI: 1.357-2.441), Model 2 (OR = 1.545, 95% CI: 1.060-2.253), and Model 3 (OR = 1.882, 95% CI: 1.228-2.883). For vitamin D insufficiency (50-<75 nmol/L), GWG >19 kg was associated with an increased risk in the unadjusted model (OR = 1.309, 95% CI: 1.026-1.670) and in Model 1 (OR = 1.312, 95% CI: 1.021-1.685), Model 2 (OR = 1.872, 95% CI: 1.305-2.684), and Model 3 (OR = 1.609, 95% CI: 1.054-2.456). This association was statistically significant in Model 3 but was no longer significant after FDR correction.
CONCLUSION: To our knowledge, this is the first multicentre study to report an association between GWG ≤10 kg and an increased risk of vitamin D deficiency in offspring, and between GWG >19 kg and an increased risk of vitamin D insufficiency. However, the latter association did not remain significant after FDR correction in sensitivity analyses based on Model 3 and requires confirmation in further studies.

Case Report: Hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia and arterial aneurysms in KAT6B-related disorder: case observation and literature perspective.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: KAT6B-related disorders (KAT6B-RD) are rare autosomal dominant chromatinopathies characterized by variable multisystem involvement and marked phenotypic heterogeneity.
CASE PRESENTATION: We describe a preterm male infant with intrauterine growth restriction who developed recurrent hypoglycemia toward the end of the first week of life during parenteral nutrition weaning, requiring a glucose infusion rate of up to 12 mg/kg/min. Biochemical findings were consistent with hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, and glycemic control was rapidly achieved with diazoxide (initiated at 5 mg/kg/day and increased to 6.9 mg/kg/day). After treatment discontinuation at 4 months of age, he exhibited recurrent hypoglycemia again, requiring the resumption of diazoxide. The patient also exhibited complete scrotal agenesis with complex genital anomalies, agenesis of the corpus callosum, generalized hypotonia, severe feeding difficulties requiring gastrostomy, primary hypothyroidism, and aneurysmal dilation of the ascending aorta and proximal right coronary artery. Clinical exome sequencing identified a de novo heterozygous pathogenic KAT6B variant (c.3995del; p.Pro1332Leufs*2) in exon 17. Diazoxide was successfully discontinued at 12 months of age under continuous glucose monitoring.
CONCLUSION: This case highlights congenital hyperinsulinism and arterial aneurysms as a clinical association observed in a patient with KAT6B-RD. Rather than representing definitive novel features of the syndrome, these manifestations should be interpreted with caution as hypothesis-generating findings potentially linked to KAT6B-mediated epigenetic dysregulation, while accounting for potential perinatal confounding factors. These findings nonetheless support careful endocrine and cardiovascular surveillance and follow-up in patients with KAT6B-RD.

title: Hydroxyurea treatment is not significantly associated with reduced spermatogonial numbers in patients with sickle cell disease.
abstract: Hydroxyurea (HU) is considered a first-line therapy for patients with sickle cell disease (SCD). In cases of inadequate response to HU therapy, patients may receive conditioning therapy prior to haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which can lead to depletion of the number of spermatogonia. Therefore, in pre-pubertal boys, fertility is preserved through cryopreservation of testicular tissue, although this is an experimental method. Analysis of this tissue showed a considerable loss of spermatogonia, leading to the hypothesis that HU therapy may reduce the spermatogonial number. However, evidence remains limited and conflicting. Therefore, this study aims to investigate the relationship between HU exposure and the spermatogonial number in boys with SCD. The number of spermatogonia per round seminiferous tubule (S/T) and the percentage of tubules containing spermatogonia were determined in cryopreserved testicular tissue from 27 HU-treated patients with SCD. Linear regression analyses were performed to assess their association with HU exposure. Spermatogonia were present in most boys with SCD, although in severely reduced numbers. S/T Z-scores and the percentage of tubules containing spermatogonia were not significantly associated with age at HU initiation, duration of HU exposure, or HU dose. In conclusion, in this cohort, no statistically significant association was observed between HU treatment and reduced spermatogonial numbers in patients with SCD.

title: The fixed cortical fraction assumption in Hip Structure Analysis produces systematic, sex- and age- dependent errors in femoral neck morphology estimates.
abstract: Hip Structure Analysis (HSA) estimates femoral neck morphology from dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) images using simplifying assumptions, including that cortical bone accounts for a fixed 60% of total bone mineral content at the narrow neck (cortical fraction, fc  = 0.6). The empirical basis of this assumption is poorly established, and its effect on HSA-derived structural parameters has not been systematically evaluated. PseudoDXA images were generated by direct projection of nanoCT volumes from cadaveric proximal femurs from 32 White female (ages 24-89+ years) and 30 White male (ages 18-89 years) donors. Cortical and trabecular bone were segmented separately, enabling direct measurement of fc and comparison of HSA estimates using fixed versus measured fc against nanoCT-derived reference values. Measured fc ranged from 0.23 to 0.67 and averaged 0.48 for females and 0.42 for males, both substantially below 0.6. In females, fc increased significantly with age; in males, fc decreased significantly with body weight. Using fixed fc produced large, systematic errors in HSA-derived cortical area and buckling ratio that were sex- and age-specific, reaching up to 36% for cortical area in younger individuals. Replacing fixed fc with measured fc significantly reduced errors for cortical area in both sexes and for buckling ratio in males, with significantly greater improvement in concordance for cortical area and inner radius in males. Buckling ratio errors remained large in females even with measured fc , consistent with an additional departure from the uniform cortical thickness assumption, which is hypothesized to be more pronounced in females due to the disproportionately thick inferior cortex. These findings demonstrate that the fixed fc assumption introduces systematic, sex- and age-specific errors into HSA-derived structural estimates, and that development of DXA-derived individualized fc estimation represents a meaningful step toward improving the clinical reliability of HSA for fracture risk assessment.

title: Efficacy and Safety of Lonapegsomatropin in Children With Turner Syndrome: 52-Week Results From the New InsiGHTS Trial.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Treatment with growth hormone is effective in improving height outcomes in children with Turner syndrome. However, poor adherence-often influenced by daily injection burden-may compromise treatment outcomes. Lonapegsomatropin is a prodrug, administered once weekly, that provides sustained release of somatropin.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of lonapegsomatropin in children with Turner syndrome.
DESIGN: New InsiGHTS is a phase 2 dose-ranging trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05690386).
SETTING: This trial was conducted across 19 centers in the United States.
PARTICIPANTS: This trial enrolled and dosed 49 prepubertal children with Turner syndrome.
INTERVENTIONS: Randomization was 1:1:1:1 to receive once-weekly lonapegsomatropin (0.24, 0.30, or 0.36 mg hGH/kg/week) or daily somatropin (0.35 mg/kg/week).
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE: The primary efficacy endpoint was annualized height velocity (AHV) at week 26. Secondary efficacy endpoints included AHV at week 52 and change from baseline in height standard deviation score (SDS) at weeks 26 and 52.
RESULTS: At week 26, AHV was comparable between lonapegsomatropin starting dose cohorts (range: 9.23 to 10.36 cm/year) and the somatropin cohort (10.86 cm/year). At week 52, AHV was comparable between pooled lonapegsomatropin cohorts (9.05 cm/year) and the somatropin cohort (9.04 cm/year), with mean gains in height SDS of 0.60 and 0.67, respectively. Lonapegsomatropin was well tolerated with a safety profile similar to somatropin.
CONCLUSIONS: Across evaluated doses, lonapegsomatropin treatment demonstrated comparable efficacy, safety, and tolerability to somatropin after 1 year, supporting development of lonapegsomatropin as a once-weekly treatment option for short stature in children with Turner syndrome.

title: Association Between Household Iodized Salt Trajectory and High Milk-Enriched Diet with Thyroid Nodules and Goiter in Children: A Prospective Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Universal salt iodization (USI) policies have achieved remarkable results in preventing iodine deficiency disorders globally. However, concerns regarding its safety have emerged along with rising detection rates of thyroid disorders and shifts in dietary structures. The association between iodized salt consumption and thyroid nodule development remains unclear, and the modifying role of dietary structures is not well understood. This study aimed to examine associations between iodized salt consumption and the incidence of thyroid nodules and goiter, accounting for dietary structures.
METHODS: This prospective cohort study enrolled 8464 school-aged children across 79 schools from 2021 to 2023. Salt exposure and dietary structures were assessed via household sampling and questionnaires. Thyroid nodules and goiter were identified through ultrasonography. Latent class trajectory modeling identified iodized and noniodized salt trajectories, alongside high milk-enriched and low milk-enriched dietary structures. Cox proportional hazards model and logistic regression model were applied to analyze the associations between salt trajectories and dietary structures with thyroid nodules and goiter separately.
RESULTS: Two thousand seven hundred and seven (32.0%) participants developed thyroid nodules and 164 (1.9%) had goiter. Two salt trajectories were identified: iodized (7892; 93.2%) and noniodized (572; 6.8%). Iodized salt was associated with lower risks of nodules (hazard ratio [HR], 0.806 [confidence interval or CI: 0.659-0.986]) and goiter (odds ratio, 0.458 [CI: 0.299-0.669]). However, the association with nodules did not persist in region-stratified analyses (HR, 1.114 [CI: 0.745-1.667]). A high milk-enriched diet was consistently associated with reduced nodule risk (HR, 0.867 [CI: 0.787-0.956]) and remained significant in all sensitivity analyses. A significant interaction was observed between dietary structure and salt trajectory (adjusted p for interaction = 0.024). A U-shaped relationship was observed between salt iodine concentration and nodule risk, with an inflection point at 21.3 mg/kg.
CONCLUSIONS: Iodized salt was associated with lower goiter risk, but its inverse association with thyroid nodules was not observed after region restriction. A high milk-enriched diet was inversely associated with thyroid nodules. These findings support continued USI for goiter prevention and highlight the importance of regional iodine status and dietary patterns when interpreting household salt use and thyroid outcomes in children.

title: Case Report: Laser thermal ablation for severe primary hyperparathyroidism in a pregnant patient with MEN1 syndrome.
abstract: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) during pregnancy is a rare clinical entity associated with substantial maternal and fetal morbidity, particularly when complicated by severe hypercalcemia. We present the case of a 44-year-old multigravida at 27 + 5 weeks' gestation who presented with symptomatic, severe hypercalcemia (3.12 mmol/L), and acute kidney injury. Diagnostic evaluation confirmed bilateral parathyroid lesions. Due to high surgical risk and patient refusal of traditional parathyroidectomy, ultrasound-guided laser thermal ablation (LTA) of the dominant right inferior adenoma was performed. The procedure induced a rapid reduction in parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentrations and normalization of serum calcium levels, accompanied by a marked recovery of renal function. Subsequent genetic testing identified a pathogenic MEN1 mutation, confirming multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1. At 39 weeks of gestation, the patient delivered a healthy infant via elective cesarean section, with no evidence of neonatal hypocalcemia. This case demonstrates that LTA may serve as a safe, effective, and minimally invasive alternative for managing severe PHPT in pregnancy when conventional surgery is contraindicated or declined. To our knowledge, this represents the first reported application of LTA in this specific clinical scenario.

title: Resistance to thyroid hormone alpha associated with a novel THRA ligand-binding domain variant: familial clinical, biochemical, skeletal, and exploratory cerebral FDG-PET/CT metabolic findings.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Thyroid hormones (TH) regulate skeletal development, central nervous system maturation, and energy homeostasis, primarily through the nuclear receptors TRα and TRβ, encoded by the THRA and THRB genes. Pathogenic variants in THRA lead to resistance to thyroid hormone alpha (RTHα), a rare and diagnostically challenging condition.
METHODS: A 36-year-old woman and her 12-year-old son were studied to characterize the clinical, biochemical, radiological, and exploratory cerebral metabolic findings associated with a previously unreported, likely pathogenic variant in THRA. Both individuals underwent a comprehensive clinical evaluation. Thyroid function tests included TSH, fT4, fT3, TT3, TT4, and rT3, along with additional biochemical assessments.Molecular analysis included whole-exome sequencing in proband 1, which identified a variant in THRA (NM_199334.5:c.662T>C; p.Ile221Thr), subsequently confirmed in the second case. Additionally, the adult patient underwent brain positron emission tomography with 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG PET) to assess regional cerebral metabolism with exploratory visual and ROI-based comparison with an age- and sex-matched control subject.
RESULTS: Both patients exhibited a phenotype consistent with RTHα, characterized by hypotonia, macrocephaly, dysmorphic features, chronic constipation, and normocytic anemia. The fT3/fT4 ratio was elevated (high-normal), and rT3 levels were decreased in both cases. The THRA variant was located in the ligand-binding domain and segregated with the familial phenotype. Exploratory brain ^18F-FDG PET assessment in Proband 1 showed symmetrically higher FDG uptake in the prefrontal cortex, basal ganglia, and lateral temporal cortex compared with the control subject, with consistently higher SUVmax values across the evaluated ROIs. These findings represent an exploratory single-subject comparison and have not previously been reported in RTHα.
CONCLUSIONS: This study expands the clinical, biochemical, radiological, and metabolic spectrum associated with THRA variants and suggests that cerebral metabolic evaluation may provide additional diagnostic insights in RTHα. Further studies, including larger cohorts and functional analyses, will be necessary to confirm the proposed mechanisms and the clinical relevance of the observed metabolic findings.

title: Real-world effectiveness of liraglutide in children with type 2 diabetes.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Since liraglutide's approval for the treatment of type 2 diabetes (T2D) in children, no real-world studies have examined its clinical outcomes in adolescents.
OBJECTIVE: Compare hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) changes in adolescents with T2D taking liraglutide in a clinical setting.
DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study from 2020 to 2023.
PARTICIPANTS: Patients with T2D ages <18 years who were prescribed liraglutide. Patients were divided into 2 groups: treated (those with evidence of taking liraglutide for ≥26 weeks) and control (those prescribed but who did not take liraglutide).
MAIN OUTCOMES: Changes in HbA1c after 26 weeks of treatment were calculated. Secondary outcomes included HbA1c changes after 52 weeks, and body mass index (BMI) z score changes and lipid markers at 26 and/or 52 weeks.
RESULTS: There was a strong trend toward a decrease in HbA1c after 26 weeks of liraglutide treatment compared with control (-0.40 [-1.90, 0.20] vs +0.15 [-1.30, 0.88], P = .064; n = 85 vs n = 30); no difference was observed at 52 weeks (-0.20 [-1.23,0.93] vs 0.50 [-1.13,1.70], P = .15; n = 100 vs n = 44). BMI z score was stable in both groups, with no differences between groups. Lipid levels were available in a small subset of patients. The liraglutide-treated group had a decrease in total cholesterol (-0.21 [-0.60, 0.16] mmol/L vs 0.49 [0.06, 0.76] mmol/L, P = .005; n = 36 vs n = 12) and low-density lipoprotein (-0.23 [-0.56, 0.16] mmol/L vs 0.35 [0.14, 0.63] mmol/L, P < .01; n = 31 vs n = 12) vs control.
CONCLUSION: Liraglutide shows potential benefits for lowering HbA1c and cholesterol in children with T2D in a clinical setting. Additional work is needed to understand how to optimize HbA1c improvements with liraglutide.

title: Limited Predictive Value of Genotype in GNAS-Related Disorders: Phenotypic Variability in a Cohort of 36 Pediatric Patients.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP) and related GNAS-associated disorders are rare conditions characterized by marked clinical and biochemical heterogeneity. Genotype-phenotype correlations remain complex due to genomic imprinting and parent-of-origin effects.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate genotype-phenotype correlations and intrafamilial variability in pediatric patients with GNAS-related disorders, with particular emphasis on familial cases.
METHODS: A retrospective study was conducted in 36 patients (20 females, 16 males) from 22 unrelated families diagnosed with GNAS-related disorders. Genetic analysis included next-generation sequencing and, in selected cases, methylation studies. Variants were classified as confirmed loss-of-function (LOF), predicted LOF, or non-LOF according to ACMG criteria and in silico splice prediction. For genotype-phenotype analyses, predicted LOF variants were included in the LOF group. Clinical, biochemical, and anthropometric data were analyzed, and pedigree analysis was performed to assess inheritance patterns and intrafamilial variability.
RESULTS: Genetic or epigenetic alterations involving the GNAS locus were identified in 26 of 36 patients (72.2%), including sequence variants in 24 patients and methylation defects in 2 patients. In 10 patients (27.8%), no molecular abnormality was identified, either due to lack of genetic testing or negative results. Among the 24 patients with sequence variants, 17 carried confirmed LOF variants according to ACMG classification. For genotype-phenotype analyses, two additional patients carrying the splice-region variant c.312+5G>A, predicted to impair splicing based on concordant predictions from multiple in silico tools, were included in the LOF group, resulting in a total of 19 LOF and 5 non-LOF patients. Patients with LOF variants demonstrated a significantly more severe biochemical phenotype, including higher PTH levels (p = 0.039), lower calcium levels (p = 0.018), higher phosphate levels (p = 0.013), and lower fT4 levels (p = 0.014). No significant differences were observed in TSH, BMI SDS, or height SDS. Pedigree analysis revealed marked intrafamilial variability, even among individuals carrying identical variants. Maternal inheritance predominated in familial cases. Notably, a clinically affected family without molecular confirmation was identified based on pedigree analysis.
CONCLUSIONS: GNAS-related disorders demonstrate substantial phenotypic variability both between and within families. Loss-of-function variants are associated with a more severe biochemical phenotype, whereas clinical features are less discriminatory. Maternal inheritance predominates, consistent with imprinting mechanisms. Although loss-of-function variants were associated with a more severe biochemical phenotype, substantial inter- and intrafamilial variability limited the predictive value of genotype alone. These findings highlight the importance of integrated clinical, biochemical, and genetic evaluation, particularly in familial cases.

title: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus And Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease In Children And Adolescents: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to determine the prevalence of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) using vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE), and to evaluate associated clinical and laboratory features.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 72 children with T1DM and 83 healthy controls who were comparable in age and sex. Hepatic steatosis was assessed using ultrasonography and VCTE. A controlled attenuation parameter (CAP) value >236 dB/m was used to define CAP-based hepatic steatosis/MASLD in the T1DM group. Clinical, anthropometric, laboratory, and radiological characteristics were compared between groups. Correlations of CAP and liver stiffness measurement (LSM) with clinical and laboratory parameters were evaluated in the T1DM cohort. Stepwise multivariable linear regression analyses were performed to identify candidate factors independently associated with CAP and LSM values.
RESULTS: CAP-based hepatic steatosis/MASLD was more frequent in children with T1DM than in controls (31.9% vs. 14.5%). Among children with T1DM, those with MASLD had higher body mass index, WHtR, diastolic blood pressure, and triglyceride levels than those without MASLD. In the multivariable CAP model, diabetes duration, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and WHtR were independently associated with higher CAP values. WHtR and alanine aminotransferase were independently associated with higher LSM values.
CONCLUSION: Children and adolescents with T1DM had a higher prevalence of CAP-based hepatic steatosis/MASLD than healthy controls. Adiposity-related parameters and dyslipidemia appear to be important clinical features associated with hepatic steatosis in pediatric T1DM.

title: Early childhood changes in BMI z-score and serum IGF-1 levels at age 6 years: the Japan environment and children study.
abstract: Body mass index (BMI) is associated with insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) concentrations in children, but longitudinal evidence regarding BMI changes during early childhood and IGF-1 concentrations at age 6 years remains limited. We examined associations between early childhood BMI z-score changes and serum IGF-1 concentrations at age 6 years in 2757 children from the Japan Environment and Children's Study. BMI z-scores were assessed at ages 2, 4, and 6 years, and serum IGF-1 was measured at age 6 years. Associations of overall BMI z-score change from ages 2 to 6 years and interval-specific changes from ages 2 to 4 and 4 to 6 years with IGF-1 were examined using multivariable linear regression. Longitudinal associations of repeated BMI z-scores with thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), free thyroxine (FT4), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models. Overall BMI z-score change from ages 2 to 6 years was positively associated with IGF-1 (B = 18.14 ng/mL; 95% confidence interval [CI], 16.34-19.95; P < .001). When interval-specific changes were simultaneously modeled, changes from ages 2 to 4 years (B = 11.43; 95% CI, 8.82-14.15) and 4 to 6 years (B = 21.24; 95% CI, 18.94-23.54) were both associated with IGF-1 (both P < .001). Associations with TSH and FT4 were weaker and inconsistent, while the age-dependent association with 25(OH)D was attenuated after adjustment for season of blood collection. These findings suggest that changes in body size during early childhood are associated with variation in serum IGF-1 concentrations at school age.

title: The diagnostic journey of fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva: evidence from a national cohort of 114 patients.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is an ultra-rare genetic disorder caused by gain-of-function variants in ACVR1, characterized by congenital great-toe malformations, recurrent inflammatory soft-tissue swellings, and progressive heterotopic ossification (HO). Early lesions may resemble neoplastic, inflammatory, infectious, or trauma-related conditions, whereas invasive procedures can trigger additional HO.
METHODS: We performed a cross-sectional analysis of 114 patients with molecularly confirmed FOP enrolled in the National Rare Diseases Registry System of China. The diagnostic journey was reconstructed to evaluate diagnostic delay, misdiagnosis, missed diagnostic opportunities, and patient-reported outcomes after high-risk procedures.
RESULTS: Patients were recruited from 23 provinces or regions. Diagnostic delay exceeded 3 years in 34.5% patients and 10 years in 9.7% patients. FOP was not considered at the first hospital visit in 85 of 114 patients (74.6%), and 72 of 114 (63.2%) reported misdiagnosis. Among misdiagnosed patients, tumor-related diagnoses were most common (36/72, 50.0%), followed by orthopedic or congenital (13/72, 18.1%) and inflammatory or infectious diagnoses (12/72, 16.7%). 102 of 114 patients (89.5%) reported congenital great-toe malformation. Biopsy was reported by 51 patients (44.7%), of whom 41 (80.4%) reported subsequent worsening; 22 of 25 patients (88.0%) who underwent HO excision reported recurrence or new lesions at the surgical site.
CONCLUSION: Diagnostic errors remained common in FOP. Biopsy and HO excision were also frequently reported in FOP patients and were often followed by patient-reported worsening or recurrence. These findings provide a rationale for prospective evaluation of an early-recognition pathway emphasizing examination of the great toes, avoidance of invasive procedures when FOP is suspected, ACVR1 testing, and specialist referral.

title: Exploring genetic variants in premature ovarian insufficiency: a cohort-based investigation of monogenic etiologies.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), affecting about 3.5% of women under 40, is marked by menstrual irregularities, amenorrhea, and heterogeneous pubertal development. Although next-generation sequencing (NGS) has expanded the list of POI-associated genes, most cases remain unexplained, and the clinical diagnostic value of gene panels is still insufficiently assessed.
OBJECTIVE: This study combines a cohort-based analysis with a critical methodological reassessment of NGS diagnostic yield in POI.
DESIGN: Prospective multicenter observational cohort study (2016-2023).
SETTING: Three Belgian academic hospitals.
PATIENTS: One hundred sixty unrelated women with idiopathic POI and 716 female controls.
INTERVENTION: Targeted NGS of 155 POI-associated genes. Variants were classified following American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology guidelines, and genes were evaluated using the latest gene-disease relationship (GDR) scoring framework.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Identification of pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants (primary outcome). Diagnostic yield of the gene panel based on genes with strong evidence (secondary outcome).
RESULTS: Pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants were identified in 19.3% of patients; however, only 7.5% were considered clinically relevant based on gene validity and inheritance patterns. Limiting analysis to the 40 genes with the strongest GDR evidence yielded a 4.4% diagnostic rate. Adding 10 genes supported by recent literature increased the yield to 7.5%. In patients with primary amenorrhea, the diagnostic rate reached 15.4%. These findings highlight the gap between variant burden and true diagnostic yield in POI.
CONCLUSION: Targeted NGS panels provide valuable clinical insight into POI genetics but should be complemented with broader genomic approaches for comprehensive diagnosis.

title: Somapacitan Treatment in Children and Adolescents Born SGA: Two-Year Efficacy and Preference Over Daily GH.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Children born small for gestational age (SGA) without spontaneous catch-up growth may require GH treatment; however, daily injections are burdensome. Somapacitan is a once-weekly long-acting GH.
OBJECTIVE: To assess efficacy and safety of once-weekly somapacitan in children born SGA, including outcomes after switching from daily GH.
DESIGN: REAL8 is a randomized, multinational, open-label, active-controlled phase 3 study with a 52-week main period and 104-week extension (NCT05330325). REAL9 (NCT05723835) is a multinational, open-label, uncontrolled phase 3 study.
SETTING: Clinics across Europe, Asia, and the Americas.
PARTICIPANTS: REAL8 randomized 142 GH-treatment-naïve, prepubertal children born SGA; 141 received treatment and 139 completed 104 weeks. REAL9 enrolled 12 children/adolescents born SGA (GH-naïve or previously treated).
INTERVENTIONS: In REAL8, participants were randomized (2:1:1) to somapacitan 0.24 mg/kg/week or daily GH (0.035 or 0.067 mg/kg/day) for 52 weeks; all received 0.24 mg/kg/week somapacitan in weeks 52-104. In REAL9, participants received 0.24 mg/kg/week somapacitan for 26 weeks.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Annualized height velocity (HV); secondary outcomes included height SD score (HSDS).
RESULTS: In REAL8, mean HV during weeks 52-104 remained above baseline across groups (8.5-8.8 cm/year), including after switching from daily GH; HSDS increased through week 104, and IGF-I SDS were similar between groups. In REAL9, HV increased in GH-naïve participants and was maintained in previously treated participants. Somapacitan was well-tolerated; adverse events were mostly mild and injection-site reactions were infrequent. Most participants switching from daily GH preferred somapacitan.
CONCLUSIONS: In children born SGA, once-weekly somapacitan maintained efficacy through 2 years, with safety comparable to daily GH, and was preferred after switching.

journal.title: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

title: Novel ABCC2 mutations in a neonate with Dubin-Johnson syndrome: a case report.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dubin-Johnson syndrome (DJS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ABCC2 gene, leading to impaired excretion of conjugated bilirubin. Neonatal or infantile onset is uncommon and easily misdiagnosed as biliary atresia or progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis.
CASE PRESENTATION: We report a female infant who presented with persistent jaundice since birth (onset in the neonatal period, ≤28 days). A definitive genetic diagnosis of Dubin-Johnson syndrome (DJS) was established at 11 months of age through next-generation sequencing. Her subsequent 5-year follow-up indicates a favorable clinical course. Laboratory tests revealed consistently normal transaminase levels with elevated total bilirubin (peak 120.3 μmol/L at 52 days), direct bilirubin (peak 61.3 μmol/L), and gamma-glutamyl transferase (88 U/L). Next-generation sequencing identified two novel compound heterozygous mutations in the ABCC2 gene: c.2443C>T (p.R815X, nonsense) inherited from the mother and c.4465_4473delinsGGCCCACAG (p.1489_1491delinsGPQ, in-frame) inherited from the father. Both mutations were classified as pathogenic/likely pathogenic according to ACMG guidelines (c.2443C>T: PVS1, PM2, PM3; c.4465_4473delinsGGCCCACAG: PM2, PM3, PM4) and have not been previously reported. Ursodeoxycholic acid therapy was administered, and bilirubin levels showed progressive decline over time; however, this improvement may also reflect the spontaneous trend toward resolution that is characteristic of the natural history of DJS.
CONCLUSION: This case expands the mutational spectrum of ABCC2 gene and highlights the critical role of genetic testing in early diagnosis of infantile DJS, thereby avoiding unnecessary invasive procedures. The favorable prognosis with conservative management further supports the benign nature of this condition.

title: Effects of combined GnRHa and letrozole on serum steroid profiles in girls with advanced bone age.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the impact of combined GnRHa and letrozole on serum steroid profiles (classical, 11-oxygenated, and backdoor androgen pathways) in girls with advanced bone age, and to monitor adverse events.
METHODS: 28 girls with advanced bone age were enrolled. Of these, 15 received add-on letrozole after GnRHa monotherapy (Group B); the remaining 13 started combination therapy from baseline (Group A). Blood was collected at baseline, 1, and 6 months. Steroids were measured by LC-MS/MS.
RESULTS: At baseline, Group A had higher classical androgens, progestogens, estrogens, INB, SHBG, and FAI than Group B (all P < 0.05), while 11-oxygenated androgens were similar. In Group A, classical androgens, P, 17-OHP, 5α-DHP, 17OH-DHP, 3α-diol, E1, E2, and FAI decreased markedly (all overall P < 0.01) and remained lower at 6 months; 11-KT showed a modest reduction at 1 month (P = 0.02), but other 11-oxygenated androgens were unchanged. In Group B, add-on letrozole reduced E1, E2, AMH, and INB (all overall P < 0.05), while most androgens and progestogens were stable. No hyperandrogenism or adverse events were observed.
CONCLUSIONS: Over 6 months, combined GnRHa and letrozole was not associated with hyperandrogenism in girls with advanced bone age. In Group A, gonadal androgens and estrogens were markedly suppressed, while adrenal androgens remained stable. In Group B, add-on letrozole had limited effects on most androgens. Estrogen suppression was observed in both groups. These findings appear to support short-term safety, although longer-term data are needed.

title: Inpatient continuous glucose monitoring halves the risk of hypoglycemia in patients with hyperinsulinism.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Patients with congenital hyperinsulinism (HI) face recurrent and unpredictable hypoglycemia. Conventional inpatient monitoring relies on intermittent fingerprick glucose testing, which is burdensome for pediatric patients and risks missing hypoglycemic episodes between tests.Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) provides high granularity, complimentary monitoring but with unproven efficacy to detect and reduce hypoglycemia in the inpatient setting. This study evaluates whether CGM can improve inpatient safety through the early detection, and subsequent treatment, of hypoglycemic episodes.
METHODS: Thirteen inpatients with HI were monitored using Dexcom G7 or G6 device. Finger-prick glucose monitoring was performed at the expert clinician's discretion and to verify CGM-prompted hypoglycemia alerts. All CGM data were retrospectively searched for hypoglycemia episodes. Fingerprick glucose data were concurrently analysed, alongside electronic health records, to quantify early hypoglycemia detection and subsequent hypoglycemia saved. CGM accuracy was analysed using established metrics, including hypoglycemia sensitivity and error grid analysis, in Python 3.1.1.
RESULTS: From 3504 paired CGM and fingerprick values, hypoglycemia sensitivity was 56.7%, with CGM devices tending to overread, by a mean of +0.43mmol/L. On Hypoglycemia Error Grid analysis, 6.2% of values were classed as moderate or severe risk.Patient data, from 627 days of monitoring, showed 721 CGM-detected hypoglycemia events (<3.5 mmol/L). Of these, 448 (62.1%) were refuted as false positives and 273 (37.9%) were confirmed as true hypoglycemia, by fingerprick glucose monitoring. Patients spent a mean of 16 minutes/day (1.1% time) in hypoglycemia. CGM alerts saved an estimated mean of 21 minutes/day of hypoglycemia; a more than halving of total hypoglycemia experienced per patient.
DISCUSSION: The use of CGM within the inpatient setting, for those with HI, allows for a significant reduction in hypoglycemia; potentially halving hypoglycemic time. Sensor accuracy remains poor in the inpatient setting, resulting in high false negatives and suboptimal hypoglycemia sensitivity.However, the overall burden of CGM use is relatively low in the inpatient setting, when healthcare professionals can share the work with parents.

title: Long-term endocrine and reproductive outcomes in female adolescent and young adult survivors after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for hematological malignancies during childhood or adolescence.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cancer treatment during childhood and adolescence, particularly hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), may adversely affect long-term reproductive and endocrine health in female adolescent and young adult (AYA) survivors, leading to premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), which may be associated with impaired pubertal development, low bone mass, and reproductive complications.
METHODS: This study included 34 female survivors treated with HSCT for hematological malignancies during childhood or adolescence (median age 10.8 years). The median follow-up from HSCT to the last gynecological assessment was 8.5 years. Hormonal assessment, pelvic ultrasound, and bone mineral density (BMD) evaluation were performed. Patients were classified as having normal ovarian function, transient ovarian insufficiency (TOI), or persistent POI.
RESULTS: At the last follow-up, normal ovarian function was observed in 15 patients (44.1%), TOI in 7 (20.6%), and persistent POI in 12 (35.3%). Patients with normal ovarian function were significantly older at HSCT (p = 0.0432), whereas premenarchal status was associated with impaired ovarian outcome (p = 0.0066). In multivariable analysis including cyclophosphamide equivalent dose (CED), radiotherapy, and menarchal status at HSCT, postmenarchal status was associated with markedly lower odds of ovarian insufficiency (adjusted OR 0.056, 95% CI 0.005-0.566; p = 0.0147). All postmenarchal patients received GnRHa, precluding separation of the effects of menarchal status and GnRHa exposure; GnRHa-treated survivors had higher AMH concentrations (p =0.0032). AMH and FSH concentrations differed significantly between groups (both p < 0.01). Uterine and mean ovarian volumes, antral follicle count (AFC), and BMD were significantly lower in patients with TOI and POI (all p < 0.05). Radiotherapy exposure was associated with both lower uterine and ovarian volumes, while puberty induction was also associated with lower uterine volume (all p <0.05). Two patients diagnosed with POI achieved spontaneous pregnancies during follow-up, one resulting in a live birth.
CONCLUSIONS: Ovarian dysfunction is highly prevalent after childhood HSCT, although partial recovery of ovarian function may occur even in patients with a diagnosis of POI. Persistent POI is associated with impaired uterine development and lower BMD despite ongoing hormone replacement therapy, underscoring the need for timely and long-lasting individualized endocrine and reproductive care in AYA survivors.
